title: Franklin's own invention went out of fashion, and Franklin had a hand in it
hook: A glass instrument Mozart wrote for faded, and its inventor was involved

open.title: Why did Benjamin Franklin's glass instrument disappear?
open.line: Dozens of glass bowls threaded on an iron rod. Benjamin Franklin built this instrument.

summary: Mesmer loved Franklin's 1761 glass armonica. Franklin sat on the 1784 commission that tested Mesmer's theory, and one study links its decline to that.

text: Dozens of glass bowls are threaded on an iron rod.
A pedal spins it, and a wet finger makes it sound.
It's Benjamin Franklin's glass armonica, finished in 1761.
By his death in 1790, more than 5,000 had been built.
He never patented it and made nothing.
In 1791, Mozart wrote a piece for this instrument.
He even played one at the home of a man named Mesmer.
Mesmer claimed an invisible force flowed in the body.
He played it for crowds he gathered.

panels.text: Bet that made it even more famous

text: Actually, in 1784 a French royal commission tested that theory.
One of its members was Franklin.
A Mesmer doctor said he'd charged a single tree among 5 in Franklin's garden.
A man said to be sensitive fainted at the wrong tree.
One paper says it fell out of fashion once Mesmer's theory was debunked.
So Franklin indirectly helped push out his own invention.

sources: The Franklin Institute: Benjamin Franklin's Glass Armonica
Gallo & Finger (2000), The power of a musical instrument (PubMed 11855437)
